h: Sebastian Ullrich fixes reference count overflow that could enable a proof of False
b: A merged Lean 4 pull request freezes objects whose 32-bit reference count overflows, preventing a use-after-free in the official kernel. The new logic is validated with a transliteration of its core to Lean followed by correctness proofs in a test file. Daniel Selsam (OpenAI) reported the issue using internal models.

h: Lean 4 redefines Decidable as a Bool paired with a proof
b: A pull request by Robin Arnez, merged on 2026-08-20, changes Decidable p to a structure containing a Bool and a proof of either p or ¬p, giving more definitional equalities and letting the decide tactic stop carrying proofs. The breaking change was possible now that the new compiler is enabled.

h: Palomar, a registry of Lean verified mathematics, opens for submissions
b: Palomar, an initiative incubated by the Lean FRO and by ICARM, registers GitHub repository snapshots after checking with the Lean tool Comparator that proofs match the claimed statements, and with a large language model that the informal description matches. Terence Tao stresses that Palomar is not a peer-reviewed journal.

h: Lean FRO and ICARM open Palomar, a registry of Lean-verified mathematics
b: Palomar, a public, searchable registry of machine-checked Lean formalizations incubated by the Lean FRO and ICARM, is now open for submissions, Terence Tao announced. Submitted repository snapshots are checked mechanically with the Lean tool Comparator and by a large language model, though Palomar is not a peer-reviewed journal.

h: Lake now fetches dependencies as treeless partial Git clones
b: A merged pull request by Mac Malone makes Lake fetch dependencies as treeless partial Git clones of a single revision, minimizing the amount of data downloaded. One caveat: Git operations inside a dependency, such as a git blame triggered by a VSCode extension, can cause lazy fetches.

h: Predictable Machines builds Predictable Code on Lean 4, open-sources two libraries
b: Predictable Code uses Lean 4 formal verification to prove that AI-generated code matches specifications, and is currently in private beta. Predictable Machines also open-sourced lean4-json-schema, which derives JSON Schemas from types and proves at compile time that serialization always validates, and lean4-tree-sitter, typed bindings for tree-sitter.

h: Guide explains how to validate and report Lean kernel soundness bugs
b: A "Kernel bug hunt" document explains what counts as a Lean kernel soundness bug and how to validate a candidate before reporting it, using lake check, comparator (the validation tool) or its web interface. Starting with Lean v4.35.0, the distribution bundles four additional kernels, two of them formally verified.

h: Paul Reichert fixes instance search seeing through type synonyms in Lean
b: Paul Reichert's merged PR ensures that, during instance search, metavariables for instance-implicit arguments are only assigned values of the expected type, fixing an issue Sebastien Gouezel hit while formalizing Riemannian metrics in Mathlib. A preparatory PR brought a clear performance improvement with no Mathlib breakage observed. Affected Mathlib declarations were fixed with a backward compatibility option.

h: Lean releases Nerodia, a library for writing Python modules in Lean
b: Nerodia, a Lean/Python FFI library inspired by PyO3, uses Lake, Lean's build system, to build native Python modules in pure Lean and generates type stubs automatically. It is a work-in-progress with a very limited API, released primarily as a proof-of-concept and to obtain feedback on its design and build process.

h: Vero benchmark tests AI agents on verified Lean 4 software repositories
b: Researchers including Kaiyu Yang, Soonho Kong, Jingxuan He, and Dawn Song introduce Vero, a benchmark of 43 multi-module instances sourced from real-world repositories, each a multi-module Lean 4 repository with predetermined API interfaces. The strongest agent fully solves only 27 of 43 instances.

h: Sebastian Graf moves VERINA contracts onto programs and names verification-condition variables
b: Two merged Lean pull requests by Sebastian Graf state each VERINA program's requires, ensures and loop invariants on the definition itself, for all 27 programs. A second pull request names a verification condition's variables after the program (acc, x instead of b✝), so proofs no longer need rename_i.

h: Leo de Moura adds a lift_lets tactic for Lean's sym => mode
b: The merged pull request moves let/have declarations of the goal toward the root as far as dependencies allow. The new Sym.liftLets implementation is near-linear in the DAG size of the input term, running 680x faster than Meta.liftLets on a chain of 4000 lets and taking 85 ms for 32000.

h: Kim Morrison releases an integer polynomial factorization library for Lean
b: The library, part of Hex, the computer algebra library for Lean, includes tactics for factorizing and irreducibility and implements van Hoeij's knapsack method, which according to Kim Morrison has never previously been formally verified. It builds on hex-lll, whose theory package proves that both lattice reducers satisfy their reducedness and lattice-preservation contracts.

h: Sebastian Graf extends Lean's def contracts and vcgen loop verification
b: Merged pull requests let repeat and while loops state the invariant and termination measure that vcgen needs, so a loop inside a def with a contract verifies without manual proof steps. Other changes allow match alternatives in ensures clauses, invariants on destructuring for loops, and type ascriptions on contract binders.

h: Claude raises Riemann zeta zero bound to 67.2%, formalized in Lean
b: An unreleased research version of Claude increased the lower bound for the fraction of Riemann zeta zeros satisfying the Riemann hypothesis from 41.6% to 67.2%. Claude and Eric Easley produced a Lean formalization that passes comparator, the validation tool originally developed by Lean FRO with feedback from the AIMO team.

h: Lean 4.33.0 released with editor, tactic, Float, and kernel changes
b: Lean 4.33.0, published 2026-08-10, makes the editor more responsive, lets try? propose proofs on its own, improves the lia and grind tactics, and stops Float from being an opaque type. It also fixes kernel soundness bugs and enables backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types by default, the change most likely to need attention when porting.

h: Ryan Peterman interviews Leo de Moura, creator of Lean and Z3
b: On The Peterman Pod, Leo de Moura discusses how formal verification and proof assistants work, Lean's role in recent math results, when software is worth formalizing, and how LLMs plus Lean will change writing software and doing math. The episode is on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts, with a transcript.

h: Mac Malone merges Lake remote cache fixes, tests, and a --package option
b: Lake now demotes cache failures during a build to trace-level messages, so builds run with --wfail or --iofail do not fail solely due to the cache, and lake cache get gains --package to fetch outputs for a specific workspace package. A new test mocks remote cache transfers with a mock Python HTTP server.

h: Lean speed site charts Mathlib build instructions across 25,000 commits
b: A graph on speed.lean-lang.org tracks mathlib4 build instructions over 25,000 commits, scaling older values to line up with newer ones across the move from the old speedcenter to radar and the switch to measuring only userspace instructions. Dashed lines mark the 90 toolchain bumps.

h: Pramaana Labs reports solving all 6 IMO 2026 problems in Lean
b: Arnav Mehta of Pramaana Labs reports that the company's system, which translates each question from English into Lean and then proves it, solved all 6 IMO 2026 problems in under 7 hours for less than $150. Pramaana Labs earlier announced $27 million in seed funding led by Khosla Ventures.

h: Yueyang Feng, Ilya Sergey and coauthors present LeetProof for verified code generation
b: LeetProof is an agentic pipeline built on Velvet, a multi-modal verifier embedded in Lean, that generates a program, its formal specification, and a machine-checkable proof from a natural-language description. The paper, accepted to ASE'26, reports that property-based testing validates specifications before any code is synthesised.

h: CSLib adds a fully verified proof of the FLP impossibility result
b: CSLib, the Lean Computer Science Library, now includes a proof of the FLP (Fischer, Lynch and Paterson) result: consensus is impossible in a distributed system with a faulty process and asynchronous messaging. Ching-Tsun Chou formalised the constructive pen and paper proof by Hagen Völzer from 2004.

h: Tim Sweeney praises the Lean team's handling of a kernel bug
b: Tim Sweeney called the response "an exemplary handling of a bug in the Lean theorem prover and proof verifier kernel." The bug was discovered in an AI generated proof, a contributor simplified it down to a straightforward reproduction, and the team fixed it speedily.

h: Alexander Gerko says AI-assisted research produced several PhDs' worth of results
b: In a LinkedIn post, Alexander Gerko says that over the last month he "vibe researched" several PhDs' worth of maths results in his former field, complete with Lean formalization, including a claimed counterexample to a top-5 major conjecture. Gerko predicts "50 years' worth of maths progress in the next 2 years."

h: Sebastian Graf extends Lean's def contracts with requires and assert
b: Merged Lean pull requests by Sebastian Graf name the precondition clause of a def contract requires, pairing with ensures, let requires and invariant bind assertion arguments such as a state monad's state, and add an assert element to do notation that vcgen proves as a verification condition while doing nothing at runtime.

h: CircuitProver uses a Lean 4 agent to prove parameterized hardware designs correct
b: Ziyi Yang, Wenji Fang, Chen Chen, Zhiyao Xie, and Hongce Zhang present CircuitProver, an agentic Lean 4-based verification framework that translates hardware designs and natural language specifications into Lean 4 models and reuses verified lemmas across tasks. Across 63 tasks it proves all benchmarks, while a vanilla agent solves 92.1% of them.

h: Amazon provides long-term financial support to the Lean Focused Research Organization
b: Amazon is providing substantial, long-term financial support to the Lean Focused Research Organization (FRO), the team building Lean, which Amazon calls the single largest donation in the FRO's history. Amazon ties the investment to agentic safety and cites Lean-based verification in Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, SampCert, and AWS Neuron.

h: Leo de Moura gives FLoC 2026 talk on Lean's design and impact
b: Leo de Moura presented "The Lean Theorem Prover: Design, Evolution, and Impact" at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon on July 26, 2026. Kim Morrison and Leo de Moura followed with a talk at IJCAR (Monday July 27 at 11:50 am) on grind, a new extensible tactic based on SMT techniques.

h: bv_decide solves 2401 of 2540 benchmarks at SMT-COMP 2026
b: In the QF_Bitvec division of the SMT-COMP 2026 Single Query Track, bv_decide reached a correct score of 2401 with zero errors, ahead of cvc5 at 2375 and Z3-GEX at 2229. Bitwuzla-MachBV led the division with 2495.

h: Patrick Hulin reports a kernel check gap allowing a proof of False
b: In leanprover/lean4#14484, Patrick Hulin reports that the kernel does not reject free variables in opaque declaration bodies, letting an adversarial metaprogram prove False with no axiom dependencies. The report, largely generated with AI, suggests applying the closure check used for definitions and theorems, and the issue is now closed.

h: Tau Ceti, a "Mathlib for AIs" from the Lean FRO, is released
b: Alex Kontorovich announced the release of Tau Ceti, which Alex Kontorovich describes as the brainchild of Kim Morrison at the Lean FRO and a "Mathlib for AIs". The stated aim is to move fast and get a whole lot more formalized math than can be done at the scale of human review.

h: Leo de Moura adds grind hom attributes to replace ToInt typeclasses
b: Leo de Moura merged pull requests adding a [grind homo] attribute, since renamed [grind hom] and [grind hom_pred], and migrated the standard library to them. The new approach will replace the ToInt typeclasses used in grind. Andres Erbsen has already successfully tried and prototyped it.

h: Leo de Moura merges grind discharger support for Sym.simp and three fixes
b: Leo de Moura merged pull requests letting grind discharge hypotheses in conditional Sym.simp theorems, preventing grind timeouts on definitional equality checks for match-expression conditions, fixing a canonicalizer bug that made grind miss valid contradictions, and fixing grind dropping E-matching theorems from custom grind attributes.

h: lean4web enables deflate compression for large websocket messages
b: A merged pull request by Jason (@jcreedcmu) enables per-message deflate compression for messages larger than 16MB in the websocket server behind lean4web, aiming to improve responsiveness of live.lean-lang.org. Full completions with Mathlib imported produce 20-40MB jsonrpc responses, which compress by a factor of 8-9x.

h: Son Ho speaks at the 3rd Lean in Munich meetup
b: Son Ho's talk at the meetup, hosted by UTUM Venture Labs, previewed Formal Spec driven Development: AI implements a spec and generates its constraints using autoformalisation, while humans write the spec and check that the constraints cover it. Lean FRO's Munich-based team, including Head of Engineering Sebastian Ullrich, attended.

h: Lean v4.33.0 release candidate 1 is out
b: The Lean developers published release candidate 1 for Lean v4.33.0, which centers on a more responsive editor, automatic try? proof suggestions, improved lia and grind tactics, a Float type that is no longer opaque, and kernel soundness fixes. It also enables backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types by default, the change most likely to need attention when porting.

h: Paul Reichert fixes slowdown caused by Lean's stricter transparency default
b: A merged Lean pull request by Paul Reichert makes whnfMatcher use the WHNF cache at sub-default transparency. It fixes a performance regression from #13895, merged on 2026-07-06, which enabled backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types by default as a breaking change that gives users more control over what is unfolded.

h: Leo de Moura merges three fixes to Lean's SymM and Sym.simp
b: Leo de Moura merged pull requests that improve support for offsets in the SymM matcher/unifier, fix Sym.simp failing to rewrite terms containing unassigned metavariables (a failure reported by Sebastian Graf), and stop preprocessType in SymM from performing zetaDelta by default.

h: Sebastian Graf adds frame inference and contract syntax to Lean's vcgen
b: Merged pull requests extend vcgen, described as a verification condition generator over the Std.Internal.Do metatheory, with automatic frame inference and with loop invariants and def contracts (require and ensures clauses) that vcgen discharges automatically. A showcase repository collects imperative Lean programs verified with one 'vcgen ... with finish'.

h: Leo de Moura adds liaSteps option and BitVec literal propagators to grind
b: A merged Lean pull request adds a liaSteps configuration option to grind, meant to quickly interrupt the search for hard linear integer arithmetic problems. A second merged pull request implements grind propagators that evaluate BitVec operations on literals.

h: Lean v4.32.0 makes the new do elaborator the default
b: Lean v4.32.0 adds the do← marker for effect forwarding and cuts import Mathlib time by about 10% through a DiscrTree insertion fix. Lake's linting framework gains option-based control and module linters, and an experimental incremental-compilation mode lands behind CLI flags.

h: Sebastian Ullrich proposes prefix trees in oleans to speed up Lean imports
b: An open pull request by Sebastian Ullrich replaces hash maps built at import time with per-module prefix trees precomputed when oleans are written, cutting import Lean wall clock by 28% and mathlib's import phase by 21%, for about 6% larger stdlib oleans. A separate pull request by Sebastian Ullrich upgrading Lean to mimalloc 3 was merged.

h: Wojciech Różowski adds two-phase stateful linters to Lean
b: A merged pull request lets linters persist and share state across command elaboration, with each stateful linter running an early phase and a late phase. Wojciech Różowski also changed the UnusedSimpArgs linter hint and split registerParametricAttribute as preparatory work for warning when @[deprecated] points at an already-deprecated declaration.

h: Kim Morrison releases first packages of Hex, a computational algebra library
b: The first Hex packages provide dense matrices, row reduction, Gram-Schmidt, and a verified implementation of the LLL lattice basis reduction algorithm, plus a version that delegates computation to the C library fplll while verifying a certificate. Specifications are written first, then AIs implement code and proofs, and a blog post runs the Coppersmith attack on RSA.

h: Sebastian Ullrich merges editor whitespace fix and deterministic kernel recursion limit
b: Lean now reuses tactic results when only whitespace after a tactic changes, so progress is kept when preparing to type the next tactic. The kernel's deep recursion error is now bounded by the maxRecDepth option instead of the physical stack size, which is a breaking change that may require explicit maxRecDepth bumps.

h: Logos Research proves an F# program and its Python rewrite equivalent
b: In a Logos Research prototype, a deterministic translator turns both the original and the rewrite into Lean, and a theorem prover proves the two compute the same result on every input. For iCPPI, a portfolio-insurance algorithm, the machine-checked proof ran to some 22,000 characters, with floats modelled as exact real numbers.

h: Leo de Moura adds rw and case tactics to Lean's sym mode
b: Merged pull requests by Leo de Moura implement the rw tactic and the case tactic (relevant for vcgen) in sym => mode, fix universe constraints and unresolved-instance reporting in SymM, add a hygienic parameter to intro-like functions, and speed up instance assignment when the goal type is ground.

h: Mac Malone merges new Lake APIs for dynamic libraries and linking
b: Lake adds Dynlib.runtimeOnlyDeps, for transitive dependencies that should not be linked but must be preloaded when precompiling, plus an API for retrieving the complete set of core dynamic libraries. A third change lets custom build targets link shared libraries or executables from a module without copying the code in LeanExe.recBuildExe.

h: ArkLib anchors a growing ecosystem of Lean libraries for verifying SNARKs
b: ArkLib, a project supported by the Ethereum Foundation, mechanizes the probabilistic security proofs that succinct non-interactive arguments of knowledge (SNARKs) depend on. It gives zk engineers and cryptography researchers machine-checked specifications and executable references for proof systems where a single soundness bug can be catastrophic.

h: Lean 4 moves deferred docstring checks onto the linter framework
b: A merged pull request by David Thrane Christiansen adapts Lean's deferred docstring check mechanism to use the linter mechanism, replacing custom CI setup with an interface akin to environment linters and governed by the option linter.doc.deferred. In a breaking change, custom Verso docstring elements now use a two-constructor type.

h: Gwern Net proposes measuring how Lean code predictability scales for LLMs
b: Gwern Net's research proposal would measure coding LLM perplexity over growing codebase context to estimate scaling laws of predictability by language. The essay predicts Lean suffers from a very high constant but would have the best scaling exponent, and so would eventually cross over more popular languages such as Python.

h: Joachim Breitner adds automatic try? suggestions to Lean at common proof sites
b: A merged pull request by Joachim Breitner makes Lean suggest try? output for empty by blocks, unsolved goals, and sorry tactics, gated by three options that default to off. It replaces the tactic.tryOnEmptyBy option from an earlier pull request with a different implementation.

h: Dwarkesh Patel relays idea of AIs forking Mathlib into parallel mathematics
b: In a post on X, Dwarkesh Patel described Grant's speculation that AIs could fork Mathlib, the Lean library of formalized math concepts and proofs, and build a "parallel math civilization." Dwarkesh Patel wrote that Lean guarantees any new conjectures would be logically valid, and that whether they would be interesting is another matter.

h: Mistral AI lists Leanstral 1.5, an updated Lean 4 proving model
b: Mistral AI's documentation lists Leanstral 1.5, dated June 30, 2026, as an updated Lean 4 formal proof engineering model optimised for automated theorem proving and autoformalization. The Apache 2.0 model has 119B total parameters (6.5B active) and a 256k context, though the page marks it deprecated with a deprecation date of 9/29/2026.

h: Wojciech Różowski opens Lean pull requests for stateful linters and unusedVariables hint
b: A now-closed pull request adds stateful linters: command linters that thread state from one command to the next, so a linter can accumulate information across a file. A merged pull request adds a hint to the unusedVariables linter, suggesting to rename the unreferenced name with an underscore.

h: Leo de Moura gives AWS talk on Lean's use across AWS
b: In a June 2026 talk, Leo de Moura (Senior Principal Applied Scientist, AWS, and Chief Architect, Lean FRO) described AWS projects built with Lean, including Cedar, a verified authorization policy language, SampCert, verified differential privacy, and Waimea, a tensor compiler for Trainium. The slides are written in Verso.

h: Henrik Böving adds cost metrics for grind's e-matching graph
b: A merged Lean pull request by Henrik Böving adds optional diagnostics, enabled via grind.ematch.diagnostics, that flag instances with many direct follow-up children and instances that participated in a large, transitive closure of follow-up instances. The metric is based on the cost heuristic of smt-scope, and thresholds are configurable.

h: David Thrane Christiansen adds extensible Markdown rendering for Verso docstrings
b: A merged Lean pull request lets custom elements in Verso docstrings define their own Markdown rendering, which is used for LSP hovers and for legacy clients that don't directly support Verso. Example uses include including one docstring in another and showing all currently-available instances of a class.

h: Sebastian Graf renames mvcgen' to vcgen and adds frame support
b: Sebastian Graf merged pull requests renaming the experimental Sym-based mvcgen' tactic to vcgen, speeding up its matching, and adding a frames clause. A new @[frameproc] attribute lets a program type register how it frames a resource, so cost budgets, separation-logic footprints, and trace invariants frame through the same mechanism.

h: Sebastian Ullrich speeds up Lean's test suite with shared header snapshots
b: A merged pull request lets about 389 elab tests that use import Lean reuse one pre-built snapshot, cutting CPU time by 26.0% (2222 s to 1645 s), with CI test wall-clock speedups of about 10-40% depending on platform. Related pull requests speed up .olean and snapshot serialization, one cutting snapshot save time by about 28%.

h: Lean 4.33 gives Float a pure Lean model, making float proofs possible
b: Julia Markus Himmel added Float.Model, a pure Lean implementation of 64-bit floating-point numbers, and made Float a wrapper around it, so float operations are no longer opaque to the kernel while compiled code still uses native operations. Users can now prove 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 with rfl.

h: Sebastian Graf ports mvcgen' to Std.Internal.Do and extends it to embedded languages
b: Sebastian Graf merged a port of the experimental mvcgen' tactic to the new Std.Internal.Do meta theory, where loop invariants no longer restate the exceptional postcondition. A follow-up extracts a WP type class from WPMonad, enabling verification of deeply embedded languages, tested on an IMP language whose WP instance has no accompanying WPMonad.

h: Lean enables respectTransparency.types by default, a breaking change
b: Paul Reichert's merged pull request makes Lean compare metavariable types at implicit transparency instead of default, building on Kim Morrison's split of transparency into implicit and instances levels (merged on 2026-06-19). Some lemmas may stop applying in simp or grind; set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types false restores the old behavior.

h: Henrik Böving makes Lean's get_task_state_core thread safe
b: A merged pull request by Henrik Böving changes the m_imp field of lean_task to an atomic. get_task_state_core read m_imp to check whether a task had finished before taking the mutex, so that memory access was undefined behavior (UB).

h: Benjamin Pierce seeks contributors to translate Software Foundations to Lean
b: Software Foundations, a series of textbooks on formal proof and foundations of programming languages formalized in Rocq, is being translated to Lean for Fall courses at Penn and elsewhere. Benjamin Pierce says the team is ready to add a few people, especially educators, and will need alpha-testers later in the summer.

h: Lake now deduplicates artifact transfers to and from its cache
b: A pull request by Mac Malone, merged into leanprover/lean4, has Lake deduplicate artifacts by their hash when uploading or downloading to the cache (for example in lake cache put or lake cache get). The change fixes possible errors when curl was asked to transfer to the same file or URL multiple times.

h: Lean 4.31.0 released with new do loops, Lake linting, mvcgen'
b: Lean 4.31.0 lands 305 changes, including while let loops in do blocks, a built-in Lake linting framework, stricter transparency handling in definitional-equality checking, and the experimental mvcgen' tactic, which can outperform mvcgen by over 100x on some synthetic benchmarks. The bundled toolchain moves from LLVM 19 to LLVM 22.

h: Wojciech Różowski adds the cbv tactic to grind's interactive sym mode
b: A merged Lean 4 pull request by Wojciech Różowski makes the cbv tactic available inside grind's interactive sym => mode. The tactic reduces the goal using call-by-value evaluation, supports at locations for hypotheses, and closes equation goals via refl when reduction finishes the proof.

h: Kevin Hartnett publishes The Proof in the Code, a book about Lean
b: Quanta Books published The Proof in the Code on June 9, 2026, in which Kevin Hartnett tells the story of the birth and rise of Lean, from a bug-checking program at Microsoft Research developed by Leo de Moura to its adoption by mathematicians and tech firms.

h: Sofia Rodrigues's pull request linking OpenSSL merged into Lean 4
b: Pull request leanprover/lean4#12030, "feat: link OpenSSL" by Sofia Rodrigues, was merged on 2026-06-05. The pull request was opened on 2026-01-16 and describes its change as linking OpenSSL.

h: Peter O'Hearn seeks a postdoc for Separation Logic in Lean at Meta
b: Peter O'Hearn is hiring a postdoc in the Meta London office who will work closely with Peter O'Hearn and others in the new AI Verification team, collaborating across Meta Superintelligence Labs and possibly building on lean/CSLib, Iris-Lean and loom/velvet.

h: The Mathlib Initiative launches Formal Frontier for open-source AI autoformalization
b: Formal Frontier is a new project focused on responsible, scalable, and open-source AI-driven autoformalization of mathematics, with XTX Markets supporting it. Its initial phase covers a community autoformalization specification, open-source tooling, and autoformalized texts chosen to fill gaps in Mathlib's existing coverage.

h: Lean's hex aggregator bundles verified computational algebra libraries for Lean 4
b: The leanprover/hex repository installs the released hex libraries at a single pinned set, including HexLLL for LLL lattice reduction and HexBerlekampZassenhaus for integer polynomial factorization. Each computational library is Mathlib-free, with Mathlib correspondence proofs in a separate theory library.

h: Kim Morrison splits Lean's implicit transparency level into implicit and instances
b: A merged pull request by Kim Morrison separates the levels so that @[implicit_reducible] annotations no longer have the side effects @[instance_reducible] has, such as allowing type class search to see through marked declarations. The hierarchy is now none < reducible < instances < implicit < default < all, and a new with_implicit tactic is added.

h: Leo de Moura adds a dsimp tactic for Lean's sym => mode
b: In a series of merged pull requests, Leo de Moura built infrastructure for a dsimp in SymM, functions for simplifying binders, reusable reduction DSimprocs (beta, zeta, zetaAll, dsimpProj, dsimpMatch), and syntax for declaring dsimp variants. The last pull request implements the dsimp tactic for interactive sym => mode.

h: Joachim Breitner adds an impossible tactic combinator to Lean
b: The merged pull request adds impossible by t, which uses the tactic t to prove that the current goal is impossible, closing the original goal as if sorry were used. try? gains an impossible branch that runs impossible by decide, impossible by simp, and impossible by grind in parallel.

h: Cajal introduces Talos, a Lean 4 framework for verifying WebAssembly modules
b: Talos provides a Wasm interpreter optimized for reasoning plus a WP calculus layer for proving program properties, with a proof that the num-integer crate's gcd using Stein's algorithm is correct. The early-stage project aims for full Wasm coverage by passing the official testsuite, and verification of any Rust crate that compiles to Wasm.

h: Sebastian Ullrich merges cross-file object sharing for Lean module serialization
b: A merged pull request adds Lean.CompactedRegion.save and read, which save or load one module at a time with explicit sharing, generalizing the batch saveModuleDataParts API. Separate pull requests by Sebastian Ullrich make Lean's CI build everything with Lake and fold the Linux Lake job into the Linux release job.

h: Kyle Miller replaces Lean's tactic configuration system with a faster one
b: A merged Lean pull request by Kyle Miller adds a tactic configuration system that supports custom configuration syntaxes, and on a simple benchmark configuration evaluation takes 6.2% of the time it used to. A separate pull request by Kyle Miller makes InfoView hovers include information about specific metavariables.

h: Lean publishes Lean Workbench, an experimental online environment for Lean
b: The leanprover/lean-workbench repository aims to provide familiar (VS Code with the Lean 4 extension) and novel interfaces to Lean online, giving each user an isolated Code Server instance inside a bubblewrap sandbox. The README warns the project is in progress and experimental, with a security audit forthcoming.

h: Lake adds a requiresModuleSystem option to flag non-module imports
b: Sebastian Ullrich's merged Lean pull request adds the Lake package option requiresModuleSystem: Lake then warns whenever a non-module-system file (one without a module header) imports a module of the package. A separate fix repairs code generation that broke with structures using private fields and types inaccessible in the current scope.

h: Demo previews Rust source references resolved through rust-analyzer
b: A demo chapter on x80.org previews foreign Rust references backed by a live language-server lookup: resolved references render a compact Rust source link and a grouped Rust code panel fetched from the location returned by rust-analyzer. A reference the language server cannot find is reported as unresolved, without a code panel.

h: Kim Morrison releases sos, a sum-of-squares tactic for Lean
b: The sos tactic is a sum-of-squares decision procedure for nonlinear real arithmetic, closely following John Harrison's HOL Light implementation. It calls the CSDP semidefinite programming library and rebuilds a fully certified result in Lean. Kim Morrison calls it a prototype and notes that frontier models have become very good at Lean metaprogramming.

h: Leo de Moura presents Lean as AI infrastructure at Science x AI Summit
b: Leo de Moura, Chief Architect of the Lean FRO, spoke on May 12, 2026 at the Science x AI Summit in Palo Alto (May 12-13, in person and online). The slides, written in Verso, cover Mathlib, IMO-level AI provers using Lean, and verification work on Cedar and SymCrypt.

h: Leo de Moura merges grind improvements for local theorems in Lean
b: In merged Lean pull requests by Leo de Moura, grind diagnostics now show local hypotheses used as E-matching theorems with their user-facing names and instantiation counters. A new grind option, genLocal, controls the maximum term generation for local theorems (for example, hypotheses) and defaults to 8, the same value as gen.

h: Leo de Moura presents Lean and AI collaboration at University of Washington
b: Leo de Moura, Chief Architect of the Lean FRO, gave the talk "Lean: Machine-Checked Mathematics and AI Collaboration" at the University of Washington on May 8, 2026. The slides open with a general-purpose AI that converted zlib (a C compression library) to Lean, passed the test suite, and proved the code correct.

h: Mac Malone merges three Lake fixes, including workspace-level compiled configurations
b: Compiled Lake configurations such as lakefile.olean now live in the workspace's .lake/config, removing a source of contention between workspaces sharing a dependency. Lake also now includes IR for a meta import's transitive imports, fixing "missing data file" errors with the artifact cache, and all Lake tests are re-enabled by default.

h: Sebastian Graf merges experimental mvcgen' tactic into the Lean toolchain
b: The pull request adds mvcgen', reimplemented from the ground up on the new SymM-based framework for efficient symbolic evaluation. It will soon replace mvcgen and can outperform it by a factor of more than 100 on some synthetic benchmarks. Join point sharing and introduction of local specs are not yet supported.

h: Wojciech Nawrocki adds collaborative editing to Lean Workbench
b: Wojciech Nawrocki merged a Yjs-based collaboration server that syncs changes between clients, plus collaborative editing support in the vscode-workbench extension. A separate change makes it impossible for openvscode-server instances to make requests against other instances.

h: Sebastian Graf brings Sym-based mvcgen' to parity with mvcgen
b: A merged Lean pull request by Sebastian Graf gives the Sym-based mvcgen' feature parity with mvcgen, except +jp (join-point handling), at a cost of about 10% vcgen slowdown for cleaner user-visible VCs. A separate change adds whileM, which makes repeat/while loops verifiable with mvcgen.

h: Jonathan Protzenko uses Aeneas to verify bounds safety in jxl-rs
b: Jonathan Protzenko's case study uses Aeneas, a toolchain for verifying Rust programs through a functional translation to Lean, on jxl-rs, a Rust rewrite of the jpeg-xl codec. The proof shows an unchecked array access always stays within bounds and showcases recent Aeneas features, including official grind support and loop combinators.

h: Leo de Moura fixes a panic and an assertion failure in Sym.simp
b: One merged Lean 4 pull request fixes a Sym.simp panic triggered when match reduction exposed kernel projection terms, for example in a do block with a for loop over tuple state. Another removes an incorrect assertion that failed on have-expressions whose binder type depends on an earlier binder.

h: Wojciech Nawrocki adds a VSCode extension to lean-workbench
b: A pull request by Wojciech Nawrocki, merged on 2026-05-05, adds a VSCode extension to integrate it with the workbench in the leanprover/lean-workbench repository. The change also adds a launch target and server endpoint to debug the extension.

h: Nathanson publishes recording of talk about Aristotle's solutions
b: Nathanson has published the recording of a talk about Aristotle's solutions to problems, including the remark "I tried to figure out what it did that I didn't do to solve the problems." Pietro Monticone shared the video on X.

h: Mac Malone extends Lean-to-Python module initialization in Nerodia
b: Mac Malone's merged pull request lets a Lean-written initializer add a constant to the Python module, adds Lean-side argument validation, and adds a Lean-to-Python-to-Lean test. A second merged change splits the global Python state (g_py_main) from the per-use GIL context (py_context).

h: Leo de Moura presents machine-checked mathematics talk at Stanford symposium
b: Leo de Moura, Chief Architect of the Lean FRO, spoke on "Machine-Checked Mathematics in the Age of AI" at the Stanford Future of Mathematics Symposium on May 1, 2026. The slides, written in Verso, cover Mathlib's 270,000+ formalized theorems, Verso Blueprint, Comparator (a judge for Lean proofs), and Lean-based IMO medal AIs.

h: Leo de Moura merges a series of grind fixes into Lean
b: The merged pull requests fix grind's AC invariants, a congruence-table panic, cast internalization order and missing proof hints. A new ringMaxDegree option (default 1024) bounds polynomial degree in the ring solver, and derived tactics such as lia, linarith and ring now fail quickly on out-of-scope problems.

h: Leo de Moura presents scalable software verification in Lean at SViL 2026
b: At SViL 2026 at INRIA Paris on April 20, 2026, Leo de Moura presented SymM, a monad for symbolic simulation and VC generation (turning code and specifications into proof obligations). On one challenge it ran about 100× faster than MetaM, and a Velvet port beat Dafny on 24 of 27 benchmarks.

h: Mark Ruvald Pedersen releases Clift, an AutoCorres-style C verification pipeline for Lean 4
b: Clift verifies C programs by lifting them into Lean 4, following the methodology pioneered by seL4's AutoCorres pipeline in Isabelle/HOL and adapting AutoCorres2's five-stage pipeline to Lean 4's type theory. The accompanying paper reports that Claude Opus 4.6 generated the vast majority of the code, with 1,698 theorems and 12 remaining sorry.

h: Joachim Breitner's experimental nanobruijn kernel type-checks all of Mathlib
b: nanobruijn, an experimental Lean 4 type checker in Rust forked from nanoda_lib, keeps expressions as pure de Bruijn indices with shift-homomorphic caching, and type-checks all of Mathlib (670k declarations) with 0 errors and 0 timeouts. The code changes were written by Claude (Anthropic), directed by Joachim Breitner.

h: Stanford hosted the Future of Mathematics Symposium on AI and formal methods
b: The symposium, held May 1-2, 2026, opened with Leo de Moura of Amazon speaking on "Machine-Checked Mathematics in the Age of AI." Other talks included Clark Barrett on CSLib, a platform for AI-assisted formal verification in Lean, Kevin Buzzard on autoformalisation, and Maryna Viazovska on formalizing the sphere packing problem.

h: David Thrane Christiansen adds a full-page search to Verso
b: A merged pull request by David Thrane Christiansen adds a full-page search to Verso, accessed by pressing enter in the search field. The page shows more results, provides more context, and has more filtering features.

h: Leo de Moura merges grind diagnostics, solver fixes, and a ring-degree limit
b: The new grind.ematch.diagnostics option tracks how E-matching theorem instances depend on each other, and a ringMaxDegree option (default 1024) bounds polynomial degree in the grind ring solver. Other merged pull requests fix beta reduction to respect the generation threshold, fix a kernel error for Nat casts to non-Int types, and extend the homomorphism demo.

h: Wojciech Różowski moves Batteries linters into Lean core and extends lake lint
b: Wojciech Różowski upstreamed the dupNamespace and unnecessarySeqFocus linters from Batteries to core Lean as "clippy" linters, which are disabled by default and run with lake lint --clippy. lake lint --builtin-lint now also supports text linters, and a new script reports deprecated modules, options and syntax usage.

h: Sidharth Hariharan, Maryna Viazovska and coauthors report on formalizing 8-dimensional sphere packing
b: The paper describes how Maryna Viazovska's 2016 solution of the sphere packing problem in dimension 8 was formally verified in Lean in February 2026, with the final stages done by Math, Inc.'s autoformalization model Gauss. It discusses the techniques used, the collaboration between humans and Gauss, and remaining project objectives.

h: Alex Meiburg shares Aristotle-authored Z80 emulator with verified assembly GCD
b: Alex Meiburg asked Aristotle to formalize a Z80 emulator, build an assembler, and write a BigNum GCD in about 80 assembly instructions, then verify it by modeling the whole CPU execution. After 14 rounds of submitting to Aristotle (without editing the prompt), the proof succeeded.

h: Alexandre Rademaker presents a port of AWS's s2n-bignum to Lean 4
b: s2n-bignum is a collection of integer arithmetic routines in pure machine code for cryptographic applications, and each function ships with a machine-checked proof in HOL Light. The CSLib Community port, presented at INRIA Paris 2026, covers the ARM (aarch64) part first, with the first two tutorials completed.

h: Lake gains builtin environment linting through new lake lint flags
b: A pull request by Wojciech Różowski, merged on 2026-04-22, adds builtin environment linting support to Lake, accessible via lake lint flags such as --builtin-lint and --clippy. It also introduces two builtin linters upstreamed from Mathlib (defLemma and checkUnivs) and a builtinLint package configuration option.

h: New arXiv papers test LLM formalization faithfulness, agents, and benchmarks in Lean
b: Kyuhee Kim, Auguste Poiroux and Antoine Bosselut evaluate GPT-5 and DeepSeek-R1 on 303 first-order logic problems: GPT-5 fabricates axioms during proof generation, while DeepSeek-R1 mistranslates premises. Other papers introduce PRIME, a benchmark of 156 theorems annotated in Lean 4, analyze tool-augmented formalization agents, and formalize the Wu-Ritt characteristic set method.

h: Signal Shot launches to formally verify the Signal protocol and app in Lean
b: The Beneficial AI Foundation, Signal, and the Lean FRO launched Signal Shot on April 20, 2026, at the Software Verification in Lean workshop in Paris, with a talk by Max Tegmark and others. Leo de Moura writes that the effort targets libsignal's Rust implementation, translated to Lean with Aeneas, Son Ho's Rust-to-Lean functional translator.

h: Beneficial AI Foundation launches Signal Shot to verify Signal in Lean
b: The Beneficial AI Foundation is verifying the Signal protocol and its Rust implementation in Lean, a public project meant to show that formal verification of major applications is doable today. The plan proves security properties of a protocol model, then uses the Aeneas tool to translate Signal's Rust code to Lean and check it against that model.

h: Dsyme's Lean Squad workflow applies Lean 4 verification to three codebases
b: Lean Squad, a GitHub Agentic Workflow, proved 443 theorems for raft-rs with three human nudge comments for about $240, and 518 theorems for Cloudflare's quiche, where it found an Ord antisymmetry violation. It also proved 259 theorems for PX4-Autopilot and found 2 bugs. Every definition and theorem statement is AI written.

h: Software Verification in Lean 2026 workshop recordings now available
b: Talks from the one-day workshop at INRIA Paris on April 20, 2026 are on YouTube, including a talk presenting SymM, a new monadic framework for high-performance verification tools built on Lean, Son Ho on SymCrypt, and Karthikeyan Bhargavan on verifying cryptographic applications. Derek Sorensen's talk was not recorded, and slides were provided instead.

h: Leo de Moura merges fixes for Lean's Sym framework and sym => mode
b: The pull requests fix a bug where satellite solvers (lia, ring, linarith) in sym => interactive mode threw an internal error, prune goals assigned by isDefEq, stop Sym.intros from assigning a metavariable when it introduces no binders, and restore eta-reduction of Sym.simp patterns containing loose pattern variables.

h: vscode-lean4 adds picker-based input method for Unicode abbreviations
b: A merged pull request by Marc Huisinga adds three commands (Find, Copy, and Insert Unicode Symbol) that search symbols by abbreviation or by symbol, making it easier to insert Unicode into non-editor dialogs. Copy and Insert are bound to Ctrl+Alt+\ depending on whether a text editor is focused.

h: Lean releases Nerodia, a work-in-progress library for writing Python modules in Lean
b: Nerodia is a library for Lean/Python FFI inspired by PyO3 that uses Lake, Lean's build system, and generates type stubs for editors. It has a very limited API and is released primarily as a proof-of-concept and to obtain feedback on its design and build process.

h: Design note proposes a two-tier design for grind scalability
b: A HackMD note proposes to "separate the cheap default from the expensive exploration": a default grind mode that is cheap, fast and fails quickly, plus explicit named tactics such as nonlinear_ineqs and fin_cases that users, grind?, or AI invoke to produce replayable scripts.

h: Verso Blueprint publishes FLT and Sphere Packing blueprints as reference ports
b: The leanprover/verso-blueprint package, for writing Blueprint documents in Verso, now publishes Verso ports of the FLT and Sphere Packing blueprints, while Noperthedron and Carleson sit outside the catalog on the retired 4.34 line. Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias's porting harness has a human use Codex CLI to carry out the porting work.
src: leanprover/verso-blueprint ejgallego.github.io ejgallego.github.io ejgallego.github.io ejgallego.github.io ejgallego/leanblueprint-to-verso

h: Veil verifies distributed protocols with a framework embedded in Lean
b: Veil is an open-source multi-modal verification framework for distributed protocols, embedded in Lean. It combines symbolic and concrete model checking, SMT-based automated proofs, and interactive theorem proving in a single tool with foundational guarantees and in-editor feedback.

h: Leo de Moura gives talk on Lean and machine-checked mathematics at SIMIS
b: Leo de Moura, Chief Architect of the Lean FRO, presented "Lean: Machine-Checked Mathematics" at the Shanghai Institute for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Sciences (SIMIS) on April 7, 2026. The slides, written in Verso, cover AI provers that use Lean, Mathlib, and grind, a proof-automation tactic inspired by modern SMT solvers.

h: Leo de Moura merges Sym framework and transparency changes into Lean
b: Leo de Moura merged pull requests adding Sym.Arith infrastructure for arithmetic normalization, fixing the sym canonicalizer, and adding a backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types option. An opt-in linter also warns about rfl simp theorems that only hold at higher transparency, part of a broader effort to ensure isDefEq respects transparency levels.

h: Kim Morrison splits Lean's implicit transparency level into implicit and instances
b: A merged pull request by Kim Morrison makes the transparency hierarchy none < reducible < instances < implicit < default < all, so @[implicit_reducible] annotations no longer have the side effects @[instance_reducible] has. A separate open pull request by Leo de Moura enables the backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types option by default.

h: Leo de Moura proposes stricter transparency default for Lean's definitional equality checker
b: Leo de Moura opened a pull request enabling the backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency.types option by default, so the definitional equality checker respects the current transparency setting when matching metavariable types. The change prevents unintended unfolding of definitions and requires adding @[implicit_reducible] and @[expose] attributes to many library definitions.

h: Leo de Moura explains in a blog post why Lean works
b: In "Why Lean?", dated 2026-04-02, Leo de Moura argues that implementing Lean in Lean lets users extend it freely, and points to a small trusted kernel with multiple independent implementations. The post also names backward compatibility as Lean's weakness: Lean code written two years ago probably needs changes to compile today.

h: leanprover-community releases a tool for offline Lean 4 teaching bundles
b: The bundle tool creates self-contained Lean 4 bundles for teaching: students download a zip, unpack it, double-click "Start_Lean", and get a working editor with no installation, no network access, and no command line needed. Each bundle ships VSCodium with the lean4 extension and only the oleans the project needs.

h: Leo de Moura publishes blog post "Why Lean?"
b: In a post dated 2026-04-02, Leo de Moura argues that Lean's implementation in Lean itself underpins its extensibility, scalability, and soundness through a small trusted kernel. The post also names backward compatibility as Lean's weakness: code written two years ago probably does not compile today without changes.

h: Leo de Moura presents the case for Lean at Signal Shot Pre-Launch
b: At Signal Shot Pre-Launch on April 1, 2026, Leo de Moura, Chief Architect of the Lean FRO, said Signal Shot will translate Rust to Lean via Aeneas, then prove correctness. The talk cited an AI-converted zlib, a C compression library, proved correct in Lean.

h: Leo de Moura presents Lean talk at the University of Minnesota
b: Leo de Moura (AWS, Lean FRO) gave the talk "Lean: Machine-Checked Mathematics and Verified Programming" on March 30, 2026. The slides describe a general-purpose AI converting zlib (a C compression library) to Lean and proving the code correct, plus grind, a proof-automation tactic inspired by modern SMT solvers.

h: Lean 4.29.0 released with a new extensible do elaborator
b: The release changes reducibility handling: isDefEq no longer bumps transparency when comparing implicit arguments, and a new @[implicit_reducible] attribute and a backward-compatibility option ease migration. It also adds grind support for higher-order Miller patterns, mvcgen support for specifications in the local context, and faster startup.

h: Bas Spitters releases CatCrypt, machine-checked cryptographic security proofs in Lean
b: CatCrypt provides a pipeline from Rust reference implementations, translated with the Hax tool, to security proofs in Lean, covering 172 cryptographic protocols and constructions (110 with the full Rust-to-Lean pipeline). Bas Spitters developed the whole library in two months working with GenAI.

h: DARPA held the kickoff meeting for its Exponentiating Mathematics (expMath) program
b: Patrick Shafto reported that the DARPA expMath kickoff included teams from CMU, Stanford, MIT, UCLA, Princeton and other universities, plus a panel of community supporters including Leo de Moura and the Lean FRO community, and Adam Topaz and the Mathlib Initiative.

h: Blog post argues Lean 4 is the greatest theorem prover
b: In "Lean 4 is the Greatest to Ever Do It", the author implements a small garbled-circuit evaluator using point-and-permute in Lean. The project combines a macro-based circuit syntax, OpenSSL bindings through Lean's C interface, imperative-style code, and a proof that the serializer behaves properly.

h: Ilya Sergey proves Move's new borrow checker correct in Lean
b: Ilya Sergey formalised and proved the correctness of the new borrow checker for Move, a smart contract language deployed on the Sui and Aptos blockchains: 39,000 lines of mechanised metatheory, produced in under a month with the help of an AI coding assistant (Claude Code).

h: Leo de Moura presents Lean 4 at NASA Formal Methods Symposium
b: Leo de Moura, Chief Architect of the Lean FRO, presents "Lean 4: A Unified Platform for Programming and Verification" at the NASA Formal Methods Symposium on May 6, 2026. The talk covers grind, Lean's new proof automation, and industry verification work including Cedar, SampCert, and SymCrypt.

h: Leo de Moura surveys industrial and AI uses of Lean at ETAPS 2026
b: Leo de Moura gave an ETAPS tutorial on April 13, 2026, then an ETAPS Industry Day talk on April 15 covering Cedar (access control), SampCert (privacy), Strata (languages), Waimea (compiler), SymCrypt (crypto), Anneal (unsafe Rust) and Veil (distributed protocols), plus AI provers for which Lean is the training environment, evaluation harness, and deployment target.

h: Mistral AI releases Leanstral, an open-source code agent for Lean 4
b: Mistral AI released Leanstral, with 6B active parameters and weights under an Apache 2.0 license. On FLTEval, a new suite built from pull requests to the FLT project, Leanstral pass@2 scores 26.3, beating Sonnet by 2.6 points while costing $36 to run versus Sonnet's $549.

h: Leo de Moura explains how independent kernels protect Lean from prover bugs
b: In the blog post "Who Watches the Provers?", Leo de Moura notes that Claude (Opus 4.6) found seven kernel bugs in Rocq and two in Nanoda, a Lean proof checker written in Rust, but no proof of false in Lean's official kernel. The Lean Kernel Arena tests 7 kernels against 133 benchmarks.

h: Menlo Ventures leads Axiom's $200 million Series A for Verified AI
b: Menlo Ventures announced it is leading a $200 million Series A for Axiom at a $1.6 billion post-money valuation. Axiom trains systems to produce formally verified outputs in Lean, and Menlo Ventures describes the bet as one that Verified AI is a new paradigm.

h: Axiom raises $200 million to verify AI-generated code with Lean
b: Axiom Quant's Series A round, led by Menlo Ventures, values the startup at $1.6 billion. Axiom trains AI systems to generate formally verified outputs in Lean and plans to scale its training infrastructure and expand its team of math experts.

h: Henrik Böving ports Lean's C emission pass from IR to LCNF
b: A merged pull request by Henrik Böving ports the C emission pass from IR to LCNF. The PR describes this as the last step of the IR/LCNF conversion, enabling end-to-end code generation through the new compilation infrastructure.

h: Joseph Tooby-Smith's Lean formalization finds error in widely cited 2006 physics paper
b: Formalizing a 2006 paper on the stability of the two Higgs doublet model (2HDM) potential, using Mathlib and Physlib, revealed an error invalidating its main theorem. The paper calls this, to the best of its knowledge, the first non-trivial error in a physics paper found through formalization.

h: Kyle Miller merges Lean syntax and structure default value changes
b: In Lean, structure field defaults can now depend on fields that come before and after them, and dotted function notation supports explicit mode (@.f) and explicit universes (.f.{u,v}). Field notation such as e.f.{u,v} now also accepts explicit universe levels, fixing a bug where levels were attributed to the wrong expression.

h: Math, Inc.'s Gauss completes formal proof of sphere packing in dimensions 8 and 24
b: Math, Inc. used Gauss to help formally verify Maryna Viazovska's Fields Medal-winning sphere packing results, proving all remaining 8-dimensional results in 5 days and autoformalizing the 24-dimensional case in two weeks. The formalization grew from 70k to about 200k lines.

h: CSLib publishes contributor guide for formalizing computer science in Lean
b: The CSLib contributing guide covers two pillars: formalising computer science as reusable infrastructure, and code reasoning about mainstream programming languages via Boole, intermediate representations, and VC generation. Contributors who use AI must explain which tools they used in the PR description, following the Mathlib policy.

h: Lean publishes fifth release candidate for v4.29.0
b: The Lean project published v4.29.0-rc5, the fifth release candidate for the v4.29.0 release of Lean, on GitHub on March 5, 2026.

h: Renaissance Philanthropy and XTX Markets add $13.5 million to AI for Math Fund
b: The new commitment brings the AI for Math Fund total to $31.5 million, with grants ranging between $100,000 and $1 million to support 12-24 months of work. Applications close on March 30, 2026 at 11:59 pm PT.

h: Kevin Hartnett's book on Lean's history opens for pre-orders
b: Kevin Hartnett's forthcoming book, "The Proof in the Code," tells the story of Lean's development and rise. The book is out in June, and pre-orders are open.

h: Math, Inc.'s Gauss autoformalizes Viazovska's 24-dimensional sphere-packing proof in Lean
b: Gauss, a Math, Inc. reasoning agent built to formalize proofs automatically, produced over 200,000 lines of Lean code for Maryna Viazovska's 24-dimensional proof in two weeks, without a preexisting blueprint. The work follows the 8-dimensional formalization announced on February 23, which built on the Formalising Sphere Packing in Lean project.

h: Emilio Jesús Gallego Arias built a Lean DSL debugger with GPT-Codex 5.3
b: In the blog post "Vibe-coding a debugger for a DSL", Joachim Breitner describes a small language embedded in Lean with a visual debugger in Lean's Info View and VSCode debugger support via the DAP protocol, built in one day of coding with GPT-Codex 5.3.

h: Rutgers group formalizes the upcoming IEEE-P3109 floating-point standard in Lean
b: Santosh Nagarakatte's group built FLoPS, which formalizes the upcoming IEEE-P3109 standard for low-precision floating-point arithmetic in Lean. The work found errors in the draft standard, which were reported to the working group and fixed, and established properties of algorithms such as Fast2Sum in the context of P3109.

h: Nick Palladinos publishes SmtLibDsl, a type-safe SMT-LIB DSL for Lean 4
b: SmtLibDsl is a domain-specific language embedded in Lean 4 for writing SMT-LIB2 constraint programs, with backends including Z3, cvc5, Kissat, and CaDiCaL. Bitvector widths and enabled SMT theories are tracked at compile time, and Lean validates every decoded SAT model.

h: Lean v4.29.0-rc1 changes how isDefEq handles transparency on implicit arguments
b: Leo de Moura's lean#12179, merged on 2026-02-16, stops isDefEq from raising transparency to .default for implicit arguments, a behavior that caused scalability problems in Mathlib. Kim Morrison advises downstream projects not to move to v4.29.0-rc1 yet, and a later PR documents the design rationale behind the transparency hierarchy.

h: Lean v4.28.0 released with a symbolic simulation framework and grind extensions
b: Lean v4.28.0 adds a lightweight symbolic simulation framework that integrates with grind and enables verification condition generators, plus user-defined grind attributes, a solver mode for bv_decide, and a first_par combinator that runs tactics in parallel. The release landed 309 changes, including performance improvements in bv_decide.

h: Kim Morrison removes the one axiom in LambdaClass's verified optimizer Truth Research ZK
b: LambdaClass described Truth Research ZK, which turns Lean 4 specifications into optimized C and Rust code with formal correctness guarantees, noting one axiom (applyIndex_tensor_eq) needed for the tensor product of permutations. A pull request by Kim Morrison, prepared with Claude Code, proves that axiom as a theorem.

h: Leo de Moura merges isDefEq transparency change into Lean core
b: The pull request stops isDefEq from raising transparency to .default when checking implicit arguments, which was creating scalability problems in Mathlib. The PR calls it a very disruptive change, reversible with set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false. Separately, Lean published the second release candidate for v4.29.0.

h: Stephen Diehl tests Opus 4.6 on a category theory library in Lean
b: Stephen Diehl built Kitty Cats, about 900 lines of Lean, with Anthropic's Opus 4.6 over two 30-minute sessions. The model handled the Yoneda lemma but needed guidance on multi-step rewrites and on refactoring verbose proofs. Diehl credits the lean-lsp-mcp server and the lean4-skills plugin for giving the model a feedback loop.

h: Leo de Moura adds higher-order Miller patterns to grind's e-matching
b: A merged Lean 4 pull request lets grind's e-matching engine keep lambda arguments as patterns when pattern variables are applied only to distinct lambda-bound variables. Previously such lambdas were ignored during matching, which limited theorems about combinators like List.foldl that take a function argument.

h: Leo de Moura adds a cache for isDefEqI results in Sym
b: A merged Lean 4 pull request by Leo de Moura caches isDefEqI results in Sym, since symbolic computation such as VC generators finds the same instances repeatedly. On the vcgen_deep_add_sub_cancel benchmark, speedups range from 30% to 37%, with goal_1000 dropping from 1663.1 ms to 1141.9 ms.

h: Leo de Moura merges two Lean core elaborator changes
b: Leo de Moura merged a pull request stopping isDefEq from raising transparency to .default for implicit arguments, which was creating scalability problems in Mathlib (old behavior: set_option backward.isDefEq.respectTransparency false). A second pull request fixes the type class resolution cache for classes with output parameters.

h: Leo de Moura tests Claude-assisted refactoring of Lean's grind and Sym modules
b: Leo de Moura opened leanprover/lean4#12448, a pull request that refactors the grind and Sym modules using Claude-assisted code transformations as an experiment in AI-aided code maintenance. The pull request is marked "do not merge".

h: Kim Morrison proposes making Mathlib's OrderDual a structure, prepared with Claude Code
b: A Mathlib pull request by Kim Morrison changes OrderDual from a type alias to a one-field structure, which prevents defeq abuse between a type and its order dual and requires explicit toDual/ofDual wrapping at type boundaries. The pull request notes it was prepared with Claude Code.

h: Ilya Sergey shows how to verify distributed protocols in Veil
b: In a February 9, 2026 post, Ilya Sergey walks through modelling, model checking, and proving the Dolev-Strong Floodset consensus protocol in Veil, VERSE lab's auto-active Lean-based verifier for distributed protocols. Veil's model checker Lace explored 54904 states, 362 of them distinct, and caught a deliberately introduced agreement bug.

h: Leo de Moura's Lean change stops simp from simplifying instances by default
b: The pull request, merged on 2026-02-05, ensures simp does not "simplify" instances by default, since doing so creates non-standard instances that cause problems in Mathlib. The old behavior can be retrieved with simp +instances, and the backward compatibility flag for dsimp also deactivates the change.

h: Leo de Moura fixes Lean's type class resolution cache
b: A merged pull request to leanprover/lean4 makes the type class resolution cache properly cache results for type classes containing output parameters. Output parameter arguments, and universe levels that only appear in output parameter types, are erased from the cache key to avoid cache misses.

h: Predictable Machines explains why it chose Lean for Predictable Code
b: In an article, Predictable Machines, Inc. explains why it chose Lean as the foundation for Predictable Code, saying Lean's combination of a programming language and a theorem prover makes it possible to formally verify that AI-generated code stays aligned with specifications as systems evolve.

h: New leancall library lets Python code call Lean functions directly
b: A post titled "Calling Lean Functions As Python Functions" introduces leancall, a Python library for Lean-Python interop built on LeanInteract, which gives a Lean REPL as a Python library. Examples include a Lean controller balancing a gym cartpole environment and a Lean ray tracer displayed with Python plotting tools.

h: Blog post formally models a Cyberchase episode's dragon game in Lean
b: A post on shadaj.me, "Formally Verifying PBS Kids with Lean4," uses Lean to model the Cyberchase episode "Problem Solving in Shangri-La," a variant of Nim where players remove 1, 2, or 3 dragons. It proves the Cybersquad's poison-number strategy wins, introducing tactics such as rw, simp, split, and omega along the way.

h: Lean publishes leansqlite, SQLite bindings for Lean
b: The leanprover/leansqlite library bundles SQLite and adds interpolated strings that expand to prepared statements, plus iterators over query result rows. A Zulip user, pandaman, shared LeanToDo, an experiment in building a web application with Lean that uses leansqlite for its database and Verso for HTML templating.

h: Sebastian Ullrich's merged PR separates meta and non-meta code in Lean binaries
b: The change lets the module system, in cooperation with the linker, keep tactics used only in proofs out of the final native binary. A simple example using meta import Lean shrinks from 130MB to 1.7MB. As a breaking change, importModules (loadExts := true) must now be preceded by enableInitializersExecution.

h: Gavin Mendel-Gleason used GPT-5.2 and Lean to verify a citation-streaming program
b: Gavin Mendel-Gleason reports that opencode, GPT-5.2 and lean-lsp-mcp produced a provably correct citation streaming program for a RAG answering system in two hours with no interventions. Gavin Mendel-Gleason argues that LLMs increase software generation faster than software understanding, and calls the approach vericoding (vibe-coding using programme verification).

h: Stan Fedotov compares two AI-assisted math papers, one checked in Lean
b: In a LinkedIn post, Stan Fedotov argues the field is "moving towards automated verification in most domains," while noting Lean is "only useful when the standard library supports your field." In one paper, only a somewhat elementary part of the proof was verified in Lean, while the authors proved the deeper parts.

h: Leo de Moura merges three Lean core changes to instance handling
b: Lean now identifies instance parameters by type using isClass? instead of binder syntax, dsimp no longer simplifies instances by default, and isDefEq no longer raises transparency to .default for implicit arguments, a change the PR calls very disruptive. Old behavior is available through backward.* options, and the PRs cite problems in Mathlib.

h: Willem Vanhulle builds a terminal user interface for Lean 4 users
b: Willem Vanhulle is putting together a TUI (a terminal-only user interface) for Lean4 users, built with Ratatui. The TUI has several display modes with different display styles for on-going mathematical proof development, and documentation is available.

h: Leo de Moura presents The State of Lean at Lean Together 2026
b: Leo de Moura, Chief Architect of the Lean FRO, reviewed 2025 at Lean Together in January 2026: 12 releases, a new compiler fully implemented in Lean, and the grind proof-automation tactic. The talk also said 2026 will be the last year with significant changes to the language and standard library.

h: Lean repository adds SymM symbolic simulation benchmark from Lean@Google Hackathon
b: A new benchmark in the lean4 test suite, described as a synthetic benchmark from the Lean@Google Hackathon, compares a MetaM tactic solution with SymM solutions, including a "SymM Solution + reusing simplifier cache" variant, on generated command sequences of up to 700 iterations, also timing kernel checking.

h: Ilya Sergey shows how to verify imperative Lean 4 programs with Velvet
b: A Proofs and Intuitions post walks through Velvet, a verifier embedded in Lean as a library and developed by VERSE Lab. Velvet discharges most proof obligations with SMT solvers (such as Z3 and cvc5) and tactics like grind, then leaves the rest for interactive proof. In the example, Claude Code and Harmonic's Aristotle each finished the remaining proof.

h: Project Numina announces Numina-Lean-Agent, an open-source theorem-proving framework
b: Yann Fleureau announced Numina-Lean-Agent, an open-source agentic framework for autoformalization and theorem proving using generic AI models. The announcement reports 12/12 on Putnam 2025 and a formalization of the "Effective Brascamp-Lieb inequalities" research paper, more than 90% of it AI-generated.

h: Leo de Moura adds ground evaluation and conditional rewriting to Sym.simp
b: Three merged Lean 4 pull requests by Leo de Moura extend Sym.simp: a simplification procedure evaluating ground terms of builtin numeric types such as Nat, Int and BitVec n, support for conditional rewriting rules, and offset terms, essential for equational theorems of functions that pattern match on natural numbers.

h: Alexandre Rademaker teaches Programming with Proofs using Lean at Universidade de Aveiro
b: Alexandre Rademaker says the course is probably the first Lean course taught in Portugal and is an official World Logic Day 2026 event. It uses The Hitchhiker's Guide to Logical Verification and is partly supported by Atlas Computing via a Schmidt Sciences grant.

h: Martin Ciupa summarizes Tom Kalil's interview with Terence Tao on AI in math
b: In a LinkedIn post, Martin Ciupa recaps the conversation, in which Terence Tao calls automating formalization (turning ordinary math into proof-assistant-checked form) the near-term change, stresses formal verification over trusting AI blindly, and highlights Lean-style autocomplete that fills a line or two at a time.

h: Axiom's AxiomProver solves all 12 Putnam problems with Lean proofs
b: AxiomProver, an autonomous AI theorem prover built by Axiom, solved 12 out of 12 problems from the Putnam Competition, 8 of them within the strict exam time limit, producing formal proofs in Lean. One combinatorial step in Problem A5 required 2,054 lines of formal proof.

h: Sebastian Ullrich proposes bundling Lean's Init library into one .olean file
b: A pull request by Sebastian Ullrich bundles all Init module files into a single file with cross-sharing, reducing cumulative size from 325MB to 264MB and openat calls for import Init on Linux from about 2000 to about 80. The pull request is still open.

h: Hacker News discusses Erdos problem #728 solved largely autonomously by AI
b: A Hacker News thread on the claim that Erdos problem #728 "was solved more or less autonomously by AI" drew 619 points and 363 comments. A Harmonic employee said Aristotle, the company's system, can translate an informal English proof into Lean, and commenters debated how to check that a theorem statement is formalized correctly.

h: Lean Community holds Lean Together 2026 virtually via Zoom, January 19 to 23
b: Lean Together is an annual meeting for users, developers, and fans of the Lean programming language and theorem prover, covering formalized mathematics, software verification, infrastructure, and outreach. The meeting is open to everyone without cost, and talks will be recorded with speakers' permission and posted to the leanprover community YouTube channel.

h: Leo de Moura removes super-linear kernel overhead in lambda simplification
b: A merged Lean pull request by Leo de Moura improves the proof term produced by mkFunext, which Sym.simp uses when simplifying lambda expressions. For a 200-lambda benchmark, kernel checking time fell from 148.681 ms to 6.903 ms, and the approach will later come to Meta.simp.

h: Lean Together 2026 schedule mixes casual and formal presentations
b: The Lean Together 2026 schedule includes a mix of casual and more formal presentations, with talks running around four hours each day and staggered start times for different time zones. Recordings of all talks are on the Lean community YouTube channel.

h: Leo de Moura adds benchmarks showing SymM beating MetaM on intros/apply
b: A merged Lean 4 pull request by Leo de Moura adds performance comparison tests between the new SymM monad and the standard MetaM for intros/apply operations. Results show a 10-20x speedup, rising from 10.8x at size 1000 to 22.0x at size 6000.

h: Math, Inc. releases full conversation with Terry Tao on mathematics' future
b: Math, Inc. posted a full conversation in which Fields medalist Terry Tao sits down with Math Inc's @jessemhan and @jdlichtman to discuss the future of mathematics. Terry Tao says this style of writing proofs shows the inputs and outputs of a proof more clearly and predicts that "the definition of a mathematician will broaden."

h: Logical Intelligence shares AI-generated verified λ-calculus to CPS compiler in Lean
b: Logical Intelligence posted on X an AI-generated, formally verified compiler from λ-calculus to CPS, written in Lean4. The post explains formal verification as code that comes with a mathematical proof, checked by the computer, that it works correctly in all cases, not just the ones tested.
